approved: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2019

The majority voted against an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2020-12-10.17.1) introduced by Tasmanian Senator [Nick McKim](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/tasmania/nick_mckim) (Greens), who explained that: > *If it were successful ... [this amendment] would require the minister, by 1 July next year, to introduce into this parliament a bill for an act to include the following professions as designated services: lawyers, conveyancers, accountants, high-value dealers, real estate agents, and trust and company service providers.* ### Amendment text > *(1) Schedule 1, page 58 (after line 22), at the end of the Schedule, add:* > > *Part 8—Designated services* > > *Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006* > > *128 After section 249* > > *Insert:* > > *249A Legislation to expand designated services* > > *(1) The Minister must, by 1 July 2021, cause to be introduced into the Parliament a Bill for an Act to include the provision of designated services by the following professions in order to address the risk of money laundering and terrorism financing:* > >> *(a) lawyers;* >> >> *(b) conveyancers;* >> >> *(c) accountants;* >> >> *(d) high-value dealers;* >> >> *(e) real estate agents;* >> >> *(f) trust and company service providers.* ### What does this bill do? Read more about the bill in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1920a/20bd073).

The Morrison government introduced the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2019, which includes reforms to customer due diligence, correspondent banking, cross-border reporting, and money-laundering offences, aiming to combat transnational crime costing Australia up to $47 billion annually. The bill also announces Australia will host the No Money for Terror conference in November 2019.

The opposition supported the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 but criticised the Morrison government for delays and failing to fully implement recommendations from the 2015 Financial Action Task Force mutual evaluation report and the 2016 statutory review, and announced a second reading amendment.

The speaker moved a second reading amendment noting Australia has not implemented all 2016 anti-money laundering recommendations, that other jurisdictions are ahead, and called on the government to avoid Australia being a soft touch for money launderers. They cited Westpac's 23 million breaches and the Crown casino scandal as evidence of inadequate protections, and criticised the government for delays and definitional deficiencies in the bill.

The speaker supported the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2019, citing fines of $700 million against Commonwealth Bank, $1.3 billion against Westpac, and $45 million against Tabcorp for breaches. They also opposed a Sunshine Coast casino, noting Premier Palaszczuk’s commitment to deny a licence, and referenced the NSW inquiry into Crown casino over money laundering allegations.

Australia's anti-money laundering bill fails to cover real estate agents, accountants and lawyers, leaving the country as a weak link in global financial crime prevention. The speaker criticised the government's eight-year delay, noting Australia's drop from 4th to 12th on Transparency International's corruption index and pointing to specific examples like Westpac's $1.3 billion fine and Crown casino's money laundering.

The bill implements overdue reforms but fails to address all deficiencies identified in the 2016 statutory review and the 2015 FATF mutual evaluation report, leaving Australia vulnerable to money laundering and terrorism financing. The speaker noted that a terrorist group in Indonesia raised US$600,000 via cybercrime in 2016, and that Australia has been named a major money-laundering destination by the United States and the Financial Secrecy Index, with high-profile cases involving Commonwealth Bank, Westpac, and Crown casino.

The Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 is too little too late, failing to address major issues such as extending regulation to non-financial sectors (tranche 2) despite years of government promises, while Australia remains a weak link in international anti-money laundering efforts as highlighted by the FATF, OECD, and IMF, and systemic breaches at Crown, Westpac, and CBA persist.

The Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing bill is supported but does not go far enough; the speaker criticised the government’s weak enforcement, citing Westpac’s $1.3 billion fine for 23 million compliance failures and evidence of Crown casino’s money laundering, and called for Helen Coonan’s removal as chair of the Australian Financial Complaints Authority.

The speaker argued that the Morrison government has failed to adequately update Australia's anti-money laundering and counterterrorism financing laws, despite multiple reviews and recommendations since 2016. The speaker noted that the bill does not extend reporting obligations to real estate agents, lawyers, or accountants, leaving loopholes that make Australia an attractive destination for illicit funds, and cited AUSTRAC investigations into Crown casino and record fines against CBA and Westpac for money laundering breaches.

The Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 was introduced to combat transnational and organised crime costing the Australian community up to $47.4 billion annually, providing law enforcement with new tools, reducing regulatory costs, implementing 2016 statutory review recommendations, and criminalising dishonestly taking credit for police awards.
